title: Are There Infinitely Many Sophie Germain Primes?
description: Formalizes the open question of whether Sophie Germain primes (primes p where 2p+1 is also prime) are infinite. Proves equivalences with the safe prime conjecture, extends the verified example base to 25 primes, and derives conditional consequences under the Sophie Germain Conjecture axiom.

openQuestion: Are there infinitely many Sophie Germain primes?
significance: The Sophie Germain prime conjecture is one of the central unsolved problems in multiplicative number theory, directly analogous to the twin prime conjecture. Sophie Germain's original motivation — connecting these primes to Fermat's Last Theorem (Case I) — makes their infinitude both historically significant and mathematically deep. Current methods (sieve theory) cannot establish any unconditional lower bound beyond the finitely many known examples.

overview.historicalContext:
Sophie Germain (1776–1831) introduced these primes while working on Fermat's Last Theorem. She proved that if $p$ is an odd Sophie Germain prime (both $p$ and $2p+1$ prime), then any Fermat equation $x^p + y^p = z^p$ must satisfy $p \mid xyz$ — eliminating the case where $p$ divides none of $x, y, z$. This was the first general result on Fermat's Last Theorem since Euler's proof for $n=3$.

The question of infinitude was never resolved. Hardy and Littlewood (1923) made the first quantitative prediction: their Conjecture B (a special case of what later became the Bateman-Horn conjecture) predicts $\pi_{SG}(x) \sim 2C_2 x / (\ln x)^2$ where $C_2 \approx 0.6602$ is the twin prime constant. Computational evidence matches this prediction closely: for $x = 10^{10}$, the ratio is within 1% of 1.

The current state of the art offers no unconditional lower bound. Brun's theorem (1919) shows the series $\sum_{p \text{ SG}} 1/p$ converges, placing Sophie Germain primes in the same 'sparse' category as twin primes. The Selberg sieve gives the upper bound $\pi_{SG}(x) = O(x / (\ln x)^2)$, matching the Hardy-Littlewood prediction in order. But proving infinitude requires a lower bound, which lies entirely beyond current methods.
overview.problemStatement:
**Question**: Is the set of Sophie Germain primes — primes $p$ for which $2p+1$ is also prime — infinite?

**Formal statement**: $\forall N : \mathbb{N}, \exists p : \mathbb{N},\; p > N \wedge \text{Prime}(p) \wedge \text{Prime}(2p+1)$

Equivalently: the safe prime conjecture ($\forall N, \exists q > N$ with $q$ and $(q-1)/2$ both prime).

Known Sophie Germain primes begin: 2, 3, 5, 11, 23, 29, 41, 53, 83, 89, 113, 131, 173, 191, 233, 239, 251, 281, 293, 359, 419, 431, 443, 491, 509, …

The largest known Sophie Germain prime (as of 2024) has over 2 million digits.
overview.proofStrategy:
Since the conjecture is open, we cannot prove the main statement. Instead, we:

**Step 1 — Equivalent reformulations**: Prove that SGC (Sophie Germain Conjecture) is equivalent to:
- The safe prime conjecture (primes $q$ where $(q-1)/2$ is also prime)
- The no-max condition (no finite bound suffices)
- A concrete prime pair statement: $\forall N, \exists p > N$ with $p$ and $2p+1$ prime

The key bijection: $p \mapsto 2p+1$ maps SG primes to safe primes monotonically. Given a SG prime $p > N$, the safe prime $2p+1 > N$. Given a safe prime $q > 2N+1$, the prime $p = (q-1)/2 > N$ is a SG prime.

**Step 2 — Extend the example base**: Verify 15 additional SG primes by computation (using Lean's `decide` tactic, which performs certified trial division). This establishes at least 25 verified examples.

**Step 3 — Conditional consequences**: Assuming the SGC axiom from the parent file, derive:
- Infinitude of safe primes (direct from SGC via the bijection)
- Infinitude of primes $\equiv 11 \pmod{12}$ (using the safe prime mod-12 structure theorem)
- No finite set covers all SG primes (using Finset.sup to find a larger prime)
keyInsights: The Sophie Germain conjecture and safe prime conjecture are equivalent via the monotone bijection p ↔ 2p+1. Proving one would immediately prove the other. This equivalence is not merely structural — it means any computational or theoretical breakthrough on safe primes directly resolves the SG conjecture.

The no-max formulation — SGC ↔ ¬∃M, ∀p SG, p ≤ M — cleanly characterizes infinitude without reference to cardinality or topology. This is the constructive statement used in practice: for any claimed bound M, SGC supplies a SG prime exceeding M.

The parity barrier (Selberg 1950s) is the fundamental obstacle: sieve methods cannot distinguish between numbers with even vs. odd number of prime factors. Proving 'p and 2p+1 are simultaneously prime' requires controlling both parities, which lies outside the reach of classical sieves.

Brun's theorem provides a weak consolation: ∑_{p SG} 1/p < ∞. This means SG primes are sparse, but the convergence is consistent with both finitely and infinitely many — it just means there aren't too many. Compare: ∑ 1/p² converges trivially (finite), and ∑_{p prime} 1/p diverges (Euler), but ∑_{p SG} 1/p sits in between.

The connection to FLT: Sophie Germain's theorem says each SG prime p gives a free FLT result (Case I holds for exponent p). The infinitude of SG primes would give infinitely many such exponents, each proved by an elementary modular arithmetic argument. This was the original motivation and remains historically significant.

sections.title: The Safe Prime Conjecture
sections.summary: Defines the Safe Prime Conjecture: for every N, there exists a safe prime q > N. This is the 'dual' form of SGC via the p ↔ 2p+1 bijection.

sections.title: Extended Verified Examples
sections.summary: Adds 15 Sophie Germain primes beyond the parent's 10, reaching 25 total. Each is verified by Lean's decide tactic: both p and 2p+1 are checked to be prime by certified computation.

sections.title: Equivalent Formulations
sections.summary: Four equivalent forms of the Sophie Germain Conjecture: the original unbounded form, the no-max condition, the safe prime conjecture, and an unfolded prime pair form.
sections.mathContext: $\text{SGC} \iff \neg(\exists M, \forall p \text{ SG}, p \leq M) \iff \text{SafePrimeConjecture} \iff (\forall N, \exists p > N,\; \text{Prime}(p) \wedge \text{Prime}(2p+1))$.

sections.title: Conditional Consequences Under SGC
sections.summary: Three results that follow from the SGC axiom: infinitely many safe primes, infinitely many primes ≡ 11 (mod 12), and the no-finite-cover property.
sections.mathContext: Under SGC: $\forall N, \exists q > N,\; \text{IsSafePrime}(q)$; $\forall N, \exists q > N,\; \text{Prime}(q) \wedge q \equiv 11 \pmod{12}$; $\forall S : \text{Finset}\; \mathbb{N}, \exists p \text{ SG}, p \notin S$.

conclusion.summary: The infinitude of Sophie Germain primes remains one of the central open problems in multiplicative number theory. This formalization establishes the equivalent reformulations of the conjecture, extends the verified example base to 25, and derives the conditional consequences that follow from the conjecture's axiomatization. The parity barrier prevents any current approach from establishing the required lower bound.
conclusion.implications:
**Cryptographic Stakes**: Safe primes — the direct companions of Sophie Germain primes — are used in Diffie-Hellman key exchange and discrete logarithm-based cryptography. The infinitude of safe primes (equivalent to SGC) would guarantee that cryptographically secure parameters exist at every bit-length.

**Sieve Theory**: SGC exemplifies the limits of the Selberg sieve. Proving it would require either a fundamentally new sieve technique or a completely different approach (e.g., via algebraic geometry or $L$-functions).

**Fermat's Last Theorem**: Each Sophie Germain prime gives a FLT Case I result by Germain's theorem. The conjecture would produce infinitely many such elementary FLT certificates, each provable by a three-line modular arithmetic argument.
openQuestions: Prove unconditionally that infinitely many Sophie Germain primes exist (the main conjecture — currently out of reach of known methods).
Formalize Brun's theorem for Sophie Germain primes: ∑_{p SG} 1/p < ∞. This is the strongest known unconditional result about their sparsity.
Formalize an upper bound π_SG(x) = O(x / (ln x)²) from the Selberg or Brun sieve, which matches the Hardy-Littlewood prediction up to a constant factor.
Formalize Sophie Germain's theorem: if p is an odd Sophie Germain prime and x^p + y^p = z^p, then p ∣ xyz (Case I of FLT holds for exponent p).

crossReferences.description: Imports the Sophie Germain prime definition, the conjecture axiom, structural theorems (mod 6, mod 12), and 10 verified examples from the parent entry.
The distribution entry establishes the counting function π_SG and its properties; this entry focuses on the infinitude question and equivalent reformulations.
Twin prime conjecture (∞ many (p, p+2) pairs) and SGC (∞ many (p, 2p+1) pairs) face identical barriers and share the twin prime constant C₂ in their Hardy-Littlewood predictions.
Euclid's proof of prime infinitude is elementary (3 lines). Adding one structured condition — 2p+1 also prime — transforms an solved problem into a completely open one.

Both SGC and Goldbach's conjecture concern simultaneous prime conditions on related numbers. Helfgott's proof of Weak Goldbach (2013) used circle method + sieve, a technique type that may eventually inform SGC approaches.
